rationale: In Baxter 2016 the CRC signal comes mostly from a few low-abundance oral pathobionts: Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas and Gemella. Each one is sparse and gets diluted among ~200 genus columns in the random forest. This change adds two summary features that work across studies because they use taxonomy names: the log of their combined relative abundance, and how many of them are detected above 1e-4 relative abundance, a cutoff that does not depend on sequencing depth.

In Baxter, the CRC signal comes mostly from several rare oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and shows up in only some patients. A random forest splitting one genus at a time combines these weak signals poorly. So I'm adding a combined oral-pathogen score built from taxonomy names: the mean log abundance across those genera and the number of them detected. It is computed per sample with no labels, and it carries over to other CRC studies.

CRC stool samples carry a small group of oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas). Each one is rare and sparse, so a random forest picking from roughly 300 genera at each split often misses them. This change adds a combined score for these four genera: their total abundance (log scale), how many of the four are detected, and the largest of them. The forest can then use the shared signal directly. The features use genus names, not study-specific OTU ids, so they should also carry over to the four external CRC studies.

CRC-enriched oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) are the most consistent CRC signal across studies. Each one is sparse, and in a random forest with sqrt-feature subsampling over about 250 genera these signals get diluted. This change adds three taxonomy-name-based summary features: the log of their pooled relative abundance, the number of these taxa detected, and the log abundance of the strongest one. That should give the forest a dense, depth-robust signal that also carries over to the external CRC studies. I haven't run it; the harness will report whether it beats the current 0.7247.

CRC signal in Baxter-style stool data comes mostly from a few rare oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each is sparse and gets diluted among hundreds of genera in a random forest. So I'm adding three features built from those taxonomy names: the log of their summed abundance, how many of them are detected, and the log of their combined abundance divided by the commensal butyrate producers (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, ...). These should give a stronger signal that also carries over to other studies.

CRC stool in Baxter 2016 is marked by a few low-abundance oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Gemella). Each one is sparse and gets lost among hundreds of genera when the forest samples features at each split. This change adds two pooled, name-based marker features: the log of their summed abundance and the number of these genera detected. Because they use taxonomy names, not study-specific OTU ids, they should also carry over to the four external CRC studies.

The CRC signal in Baxter comes mostly from a small group of oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each is rare and patchy on its own, so the random forest struggles to pick them up genus by genus. This change adds two pooled features built from those genus names: the log of their combined relative abundance and how many of them are detected. Because they rely on taxonomy names rather than study-specific OTU ids, they should carry over to the four external CRC studies.

The CRC signal in Baxter comes mostly from a handful of rare oral-pathogen genera (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and gets diluted among hundreds of genus features in the random forest. This change adds three summary features for that group: total relative abundance, number of marker genera detected, and mean log-abundance. They are built from taxonomy names, so they should also carry over to the external studies.

CRC stool shows an enrichment of low-abundance oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella). With ~200 genus columns and sqrt feature subsampling, the random forest rarely picks up these weak individual signals. This change adds two features built from these genera, matched by taxonomy name so they also work in other studies: their summed log relative abundance, and how many of them are detected.

The CRC signal in Baxter 2016 comes mostly from a few rare oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas) that tend to show up together in tumours. A random forest splits on one genus at a time and can't easily add up four sparse, low-abundance signals. So I add two composite features built from taxonomy names, which keeps them usable on the other CRC studies: the log of the summed oral-pathogen relative abundance, and the number of those genera detected (a presence count, which is robust to sequencing depth).

CRC in Baxter is driven by a few rare oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and noisy, so random forest splits on single genera don't capture them well. This change adds two marker features built from taxonomy names, so they also carry over to the external studies: the pooled log abundance of these taxa and how many of them are present. A single strong composite feature should improve the forest's AUROC.

Baxter's CRC signal comes mostly from a few oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas). Spread across ~250 genera, these sparse features rarely get picked by the random forest. I'm adding two features built from taxonomy names, which keeps them transferable to other studies: a combined log-abundance score for these markers and a count of how many are present.

Baxter-type CRC signals come mainly from a few low-abundance oral pathogens (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella). A random forest over about 200 genera rarely splits on any one of them, so I add a combined "oral-pathogen marker score" built from genus names: the log total abundance of these genera plus how many are present. The feature uses names, not study-specific OTU ids, so it should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

Add composite features for the known oral-pathogen CRC marker group (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas/Micromonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella, Solobacterium). The features are the log of their summed relative abundance and the number of these genera detected. Each marker is sparse and rarely chosen among the ~250 genus splits the random forest sees, but together they form a strong signal. Because the features use genus names, they should also carry over to the external CRC studies.

The main CRC signal is a small group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, plus Gemella and Solobacterium). Each one is rare and only present in some samples, so a random forest seldom picks any single one of them for a split. I'm adding combined marker features matched on taxonomy names (pooled log abundance and how many markers are present), which concentrates that signal and should still work on the external CRC studies. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

CRC signal in Baxter comes from a handful of rare oral taxa (Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus), plus broader shifts at family and order level that genus-only features split across many sparse columns. I'm adding abundance features summed over each full taxonomic lineage from phylum down to genus, so the random forest can split on coarser clades. A 5% prevalence filter on the training fold removes noise taxa that dilute the forest's feature sampling. The features use taxonomy names only, so they should still transfer to the other CRC studies.

Baxter's CRC signal mostly comes from a handful of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each is rare and sparse, so a random forest seldom picks any single one among about 250 genera. I'm adding two features computed only from genus names: a combined log-abundance score for these pathobionts and a count of how many are present. The forest can then use their joint signal directly, and both features carry over to the external studies.

CRC's best-replicated stool signal is a group of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Parvimonas, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each is rare and patchy, so the RF hardly ever picks any single one out of hundreds of genera. I'm adding a few summary features for this group: their combined abundance (raw and log) and how many of the five are present. This should give a stronger and more robust split, and because it uses genus names it should carry over to the external studies.

Baxter 2016 found that the CRC signal comes mostly from a few rare oral-pathogen genera: Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus and Porphyromonas. Among about 250 genera, a random forest rarely gets to split on these sparse features. This change adds two marker features: the summed log relative abundance of these genera and how many of them are detected. Both are built from taxonomy names, so the same features should work on the external CRC studies.

The CRC signal in Baxter comes mainly from a small group of oral pathogens that are rare and often absent: Fusobacterium, Porphyromonas, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus and Gemella. A random forest working on ~150 sparse genus columns rarely gets to use them together. This change adds a combined "oral-pathogen" score: the log of the summed abundance of those genera, plus a count of how many are detected. That pools weak, separate signals into one strong split, and because it uses taxonomy names rather than study-specific OTU ids, it should also carry over to the external CRC studies.
